'''''Euphorbia tithymaloides''''' is a [[Perennial plant|perennial]] [[succulent]] [[spurge]] native to the [[Tropics|tropical]] and [[Subtropics|subtropical]] areas of [[North America]] and [[Central America]].<ref>Sajeva and Costanzo, ''Succulents: The Illustrated Dictionary'', 1994, p. 185.</ref> An erect [[shrub]],<ref name="Vardhana">Vardhana, ''Direct Uses of Medicinal Plants and Their Identification'', 2008, p. 261.</ref> the plant is also known by the scientific name ''Pedilanthus tithymaloides''. However, the genus ''[[Pedilanthus]]'' has been subsumed into the genus ''Euphorbia'', and is more correctly known by its new name (''Euphorbia tithymaloides'').<ref name="Steinmann">Steinmann, "The Submersion of ''Pedilanthus'' into ''Euphorbia'' (Euphorbiaceae)," ''Acta Botanica Mexicana'', 2003, p. 45.</ref><ref name="Toxicity181">Spoerke and Smolinske, ''Toxicity of Houseplants'', 1990, p. 181.</ref>

== Names ==
''Euphorbia tithymaloides'' has a large number of household names used by gardeners and the public. Among them are '''redbird flower''',<ref>{{PLANTS|id=PETI|taxon=Pedilanthus tithymaloides|accessdate=31 January 2016}}</ref> '''devil's-backbone''',<ref name=BSBI07>{{BSBI 2007 |access-date=2014-10-17 }}</ref> '''redbird cactus''', '''Jewbush''', '''buck-thorn''', '''cimora misha''', '''Christmas candle''', '''fiddle flower''', '''ipecacuahana''', '''Jacob's ladder''', '''Japanese poinsettia''', '''Jew's slipper''', '''milk-hedge''', '''myrtle-leaved spurge''', '''Padus-leaved clipper plant, ''' '''red slipper spurge''', '''slipper flower''', '''slipper plant''', '''slipper spurge''', '''timora misha''', and '''zig-zag plant'''.<ref name="Toxicity181" /><ref>Nellis, ''Poisonous Plants and Animals of Florida and the Caribbean'', 1997, p. 182-183.</ref><ref>Balfour, ''Cyclopædia of India and of Eastern and Southern Asia Commercial, Industrial and Scientific...,'' 1873, p. 77; Strong, ''The American Flora: Or History of Plants and Wild Flowers'', 1850, p. 126; Datta, ''Systematic Botany'', 1988, p. 321.</ref>

In other parts of the world, it is known as '''gin-ryu''' (Japan); '''pokok lipan''' and '''penawar lipan''' (Indonesia); '''airi''', '''baire''', and '''agia''' "rang chita" (Bengal), (India); '''{{transliteration|yo|italic=no|aperejo}}''' (Yoruba); '''sapatinho do diabo''' (Brazil); '''ítamo real''' (Cuba and Puerto Rico); '''pantoufle''' (France); and '''zapatilla del diablo''' (Mexico).<ref>Quattrocchi, ''CRC World Dictionary of Plant Names: Common Names, Scientific Names, Eponyms, and Etymology'', 1990, p. 1987; Torkelson, ''The Cross Name Index to Medicinal Plants: Common Names, M-Z'', 1996, p. 716.</ref><ref name="Liogier">Liogier and Martorell, ''Flora of Puerto Rico and Adjacent Islands: A Systematic Synopsis'', 2000, p. 105.</ref>

== Description ==
[[File:Euphorbia tithymaloides Variegatus kz1.jpg|thumb|left|Leaves]]
The shrub can grow to {{convert|6|to|8|ft|m|1|order=flip}} in height and generally is about {{convert|18|to|24|in|cm|abbr=on|order=flip|round=5}} in width.<ref name="Millspaugh">[https://books.google.com/books?id=fchgAAAAMAAJ&dq=%22Euphorbia+tithymaloides%22+herb&pg=PA355 Millspaugh and Hamet, ''The Genera "Pedilanthus" and "Cubanthus," and Other American "Euphorbiaceae"'', 1913, p. 355.]</ref> The leaf is a [[Leaf#Divisions of the blade|simple]] [[Leaf#Basic types|angiosperm]] leaf, arranged [[Leaf#Arrangement on the stem|oppositely]] on the stem.<ref name="Vardhana" /><ref name="Millspaugh" /> Each leaf is [[Leaf#Characteristics of the petiole|sessile]] (attaching directly to the plant), and about {{convert|1.4|to|3|in|mm|order=flip|abbr=on|round=5}} in length.<ref name="Vardhana" /><ref name="Millspaugh" /> The leaves are [[Leaf#Surface|glabrous]] (smooth) and [[Leaf shape|acuminate]] in shape, with [[Leaf#Edge|entire]] (smooth) edges.<ref name="Vardhana" /><ref name="Millspaugh" /> The veins in the leaves are [[Leaf#Venation|pinnate]].<ref name="Vardhana" /><ref name="Millspaugh" />

===Inflorescences=== 
The plant terminates in a [[Inflorescence#Determinate or Cymose|dichotomous cyme]], with a [[Peduncle (botany)|peduncle]] supporting each flower.<ref name="Vardhana" /><ref name="Millspaugh" /> The floral leaves are bifid (split in two parts) and [[Leaf shape|ovate]], while the [[Bract|involucral bracts]] are bright red, irregularly [[Leaf shape|acuminate]] in shape (e.g., like a slipper), and about {{convert|0.043|to|0.051|in|mm|order=flip|abbr=on}} in length with a long, thin tube.<ref name="Vardhana" /><ref name="Millspaugh" /> The flower is void of scent.<ref name="Strong127">Strong, ''The American Flora: Or History of Plants and Wild Flowers'', 1850, p. 127.</ref> The male [[Pedicel (botany)|pedicel]] is hairy, while the female is glabrous.<ref name="Millspaugh" /> The plant generally flowers in mid-spring.<ref name="Vardhana" />

The seed pod is about {{convert|0.30|in|mm|order=flip|abbr=on|round=0.5}} long and {{convert|0.35|in|mm|order=flip|abbr=on|round=0.5}} wide, and ovoid in shape (with truncated ends).<ref name="Millspaugh" />

== Cultivation ==
[[File:Devil's Backbone (Euphorbia tithymaloides).jpg|thumb|Variegated variety with pink flushes]]
[[File:Euphorbia tithymaloides in Batu Pahat 20250204 145651.jpg|thumb|Curled leaves of ''E. tithymaloides''.]]
''Euphorbia tithymaloides'' was introduced as a garden plant prior to 1688.<ref name="Wijands">Wijnands, ''The Botany of the Commelins'', 1983, p. 105.</ref> The first record of it growing in a garden was in Amsterdam.<ref name="Wijands" /> It is primarily used as an outdoor garden border plant,<ref name="Liogier" /> but certain varieties do well indoors.<ref name="Pienaar" /> Because of the plant's toxicity, gardeners are cautioned to wear goggles, gloves, long-sleeved shirts, and long pants.<ref name="Nellis182">Nellis, ''Poisonous Plants and Animals of Florida and the Caribbean'', 1997, p. 182.</ref>

Propagation may be by seed or cutting. Cuttings should be made above a joint, be {{convert|5|to|6|in|cm}} long, and planted in sandy, nutrient-rich soil and allowed to root before planting.<ref name="Strong127" /> Cuttings should be made in March – April or June – July, and from the middle or top of the main stem.<ref>Neumann, Kumar, and Sopory, ''Recent Advances in Plant Biotechnology and Its Applications'', 2008, p. 352.</ref> [[Hummingbird]]s are attracted to the plant's flowers.<ref name="Nellis182" /> [[Cabbage worm]]s are particularly fond of the plant's leaves.

It prefers soil that is sandy, well-drained, and nutrient-rich, particularly with higher concentrations of [[boron]], [[copper]], [[iron]], [[manganese]], [[molybdenum]], and [[zinc]].<ref name="Pienaar">Pienaar, ''The South African "What Flower Is That?"'', 2000, p. 253.</ref><ref name="Neumann354">Neumann, Kumar, and Sopory, ''Recent Advances in Plant Biotechnology and Its Applications'', 2008, p. 354.</ref> It is relatively intolerant of high [[soil salinity]] levels, but exhibits saline tolerance if well fertilized.<ref name="Neumann354" /> The plant tends to be taller and have more biomass if it is well-watered.<ref name="Neumann354" /> The plant requires a sunny area to grow in.<ref name="Pienaar" /> Municipalities have planted ''Euphorbia tithymaloides'' in [[landfill]]s, toxic waste sites, and along roadsides because it is one of the few plants which can thrive in these more difficult environments.<ref name="Liogier" /><ref name="Neumann354" />

== Toxicity ==

The roots, stems, and leaves of the plant are known to be toxic.<ref name="Toxicity181" /><ref name="Nellis182" /> These parts of the plant contain [[euphorbol]] (a complex [[terpene]]) and other [[diterpene]] [[ester]]s.<ref name="Toxicity181" /><ref name="Nellis182" /> These are also known [[carcinogen]]s.<ref name="Toxicity181" /><ref name="Nellis182" /> The plant's leaves and stems also contain [[beta-sitosterol]], [[cycloartenone]], [[octacosanol]], and [[oxime]], all of which have known medicinal as well as toxic properties.<ref name="Khare">Khare, ''Indian Medicinal Plants: An Illustrated Dictionary'', 2007, p. 469.</ref>

Even minor amounts (a few drops) of the juice of the ''Euphorbia tithymaloides'' root can irritate mucosal membranes.<ref name="Nellis182" /> When ingested, the irritation of the mucosal membranes of the stomach and intestines will cause nausea and vomiting.<ref name="Toxicity181" /><ref name="Nellis182" /> Topical application causes skin irritation, [[inflammation]], and even blisters.<ref name="Toxicity181" /><ref name="Nellis182" /> If introduced topically to the eye, severe pain, [[keratoconjunctivitis]], and reduced visual acuity occur.<ref name="Toxicity181" /><ref name="Nellis182" /> Ingesting even a few seeds can cause violent and persistent vomiting and extreme [[diarrhea]].<ref name="Nellis182" />

If latex or root juice gets on the skin, the victim should immediately wash with soap and warm water.<ref name="Nellis182" /> If [[latex]] or juice gets in the eye, continuous rinsing with fresh water should be the first course of action.<ref name="Nellis182" /> Topical steroids are indicated for skin or eye contact.<ref name="Nellis182" /> Intravenous fluids are often administered to counteract the fluid loss due to vomiting and diarrhea.<ref name="Nellis182" />

== Uses==
===Medicinal===
The root is known to be a powerful [[emetic]].<ref name="Vardhana" /><ref name="Nellis182" /> A [[Protease|proteolytic enzyme]] known as [[pedilanthain]] can be extracted from the plant's latex, and has been shown in experiments to be effective against intestinal worms and to reduce inflammation when ingested.<ref name="Nellis182" /><ref name="Khare" /> In 1995, a [[galactose]]-specific [[lectin]] was purified from the plant's latex, and indications are that it might be useful in combatting [[diabetes mellitus]].<ref>Van Damme, ''Handbook of Plant Lectins: Properties and Biomedical Applications'', 1998, p. 211; Nagda and Deshmukh, "Hemagglutination Pattern of Galactose Specific Lectin From ''Pedilanthus tithymaloides'' in Diabetes Mellitus," ''Indian Journal of Experimental Biology'', 1998, 426-428.</ref>

In [[folk medicine]], tea has been brewed from the leaves which has been used to treat [[asthma]], persistent coughing, [[laryngitis]], [[mouth ulcer]]s, and [[venereal disease]].<ref name="Nellis182" /> Tea brewed from the root has been used as an [[abortifacient]].<ref name="Nellis182" /> The latex has been used topically to treat [[callus]]es, ear ache, insect stings, [[ringworm]], [[skin cancer]], toothache, [[umbilical hernia]]s, and [[wart]]s.<ref name="Nellis182" /> None of these uses has been scientifically verified as effective.<ref name="Nellis182" /> In the [[West Indies]], a few drops of the latex is added to milk and used as an emetic.<ref name="Toxicity181" />

=== Other uses ===

In [[Peru]], the plant is known as "cimora misha", "timora misha", or "planta magica". It is sometimes added to drinks made from [[mescaline]]-containing [[Trichocereus]] cacti (although ''Euphorbia tithymaloides'' has no known [[Psychoactive drug|psychoactive]] properties).<ref>Anderson, ''The Cactus Family'', 2001, p. 49.</ref> In Bengal, India, the species has been known as "rang chita".<ref>Kumudranjan Naskar, Plant Wealth of the Lower Ganga Delta: An Eco-taxonomical Approach, Volume 2, p. 589.</ref>

The fast-growing nature of the plant, coupled with its ability to grow in relatively toxic soils, had led scientists in [[India]] to investigate its usefulness as a "petrocrop", a plant which could yield [[biofuel]] compounds for [[internal combustion engine]]s.<ref name="Neumann354" /><ref>Chandra and Kehri, ''Biotechnology of "Va mycorrhiza": Indian Scenario'', 2006, p. 268.</ref>

== Taxonomy ==
{{As of|2024|8}}, [[Plants of the World Online]] recognises eight subspecies, as follows:{{R|POWO}}
*''Euphorbia tithymaloides'' subsp. ''angustifolia'' {{small|(Poit.) [[Victor W. Steinmann|V.W.Steinm.]]}}
*''Euphorbia tithymaloides'' subsp. ''bahamensis'' {{small|([[Charles Frederick Millspaugh|Millsp.]]) [[Rafaël Govaerts|Govaerts]]}}
*''Euphorbia tithymaloides'' subsp. ''jamaicensis'' {{small|(Millsp. & [[Nathaniel Lord Britton|Britton]]) V.W.Steinm.}}
*''Euphorbia tithymaloides'' subsp. ''padifolia'' {{small|(L.) V.W.Steinm.}}
*''Euphorbia tithymaloides'' subsp. ''parasitica'' {{small|([[Pierre Edmond Boissier|Boiss.]] ex [[Johann Friedrich Klotzsch|Klotzsch]]) V.W.Steinm.}}
*''Euphorbia tithymaloides'' subsp. ''retusa'' {{small|([[George Bentham|Benth.]]) V.W.Steinm.}}
*''Euphorbia tithymaloides'' subsp. ''smallii'' {{small|(Millsp.) V.W.Steinm.}}
*''Euphorbia tithymaloides'' subsp. ''tithymaloides''

Subspecies are usually identifiable by their leaves, which come in several types such as [[Lauraceae|laurel]]-like and variegated and which can be tinged with white or red.<ref name="Pienaar" /><ref name="Strong127" />

=== Status as a ring species ===
In 2012, Cacho and Baum showed that ''Euphorbia tithymaloides'' is a [[ring species]], the first example known among the plants.<ref>Cacho & Baum (2012) "[http://rspb.royalsocietypublishing.org/content/early/2012/06/11/rspb.2012.0498 The Caribbean slipper spurge Euphorbia tithymaloides: the first example of a ring species in plants]", Proceedings of the Royal Society B</ref> It has reproduced and evolved, spreading in a forked pattern along either side of the [[Caribbean]] basin, through [[Central America]] and the Caribbean, and meeting again in the [[Virgin Islands]], where the two fronts there reunited appear to be morphologically and ecologically distinct.
